State-dependent modulation of spiny projection neurons controls levodopa-induced dyskinesia in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease¶

This notebook shows how to find and read the files of DANDI:001538, the data of Zhai et al. 2025 from the Surmeier lab. The lab studied levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) in mice with a unilateral 6-OHDA lesion, a model of Parkinson's disease. The dataset holds:

  • Patch-clamp recordings from striatal spiny projection neurons (dSPNs and iSPNs), with two-photon line scans of their dendrites
  • Sr2+-oEPSC recordings: voltage-clamp currents evoked by optogenetic stimulation of cortical terminals
  • GRAB-ACh3.0 two-photon imaging of acetylcholine release
  • Abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) ratings and videos of the mice after levodopa
  • Two-photon and confocal images of dendritic spines

Streaming files from DANDI¶

The files can be read directly from the archive without downloading them. We list the dandiset's NWB files and define a function that opens one by its path.

In [2]:
import h5py
import remfile
from dandi.dandiapi import DandiAPIClient
from pynwb import NWBHDF5IO

dandiset = DandiAPIClient().get_dandiset("001538", "0.261124.1858")
assets = {asset.path: asset for asset in dandiset.get_assets() if asset.path.endswith(".nwb")}
print(f"{len(assets)} NWB files")


def open_nwbfile(asset_path):
    """Stream one NWB file from DANDI without downloading it."""
    url = assets[asset_path].get_content_url(follow_redirects=1, strip_query=True)
    io = NWBHDF5IO(file=h5py.File(remfile.File(url), "r"), load_namespaces=True)
    return io.read()

391 NWB files

Finding files¶

Each file's path on DANDI has the form

sub-<subject_id>/sub-<subject_id>_ses-<session_id>_<modalities>.nwb

The session ID has five parts joined by ++:

<cell type>++<state>++<pharmacology>++<genotype>++<date>

For example, dSPN++OnState++D1RaSch++WT++20190411 is a recording of dSPNs from a wild-type mouse in the LID on-state, with the D1 receptor antagonist SCH 23390, on 2019-04-11. Recordings that do not target one cell type (behaviour, acetylcholine imaging) have pan as the cell type.

The modalities suffix lists the kinds of data in the file, for example icephys for patch clamp and ophys for imaging. The helpers below read these parts from a path.

In [3]:
from collections import Counter


def get_session_id(asset_path):
    """The session ID of a DANDI asset path, between '_ses-' and the modalities suffix."""
    file_name = asset_path.split("/")[-1].removesuffix(".nwb")
    return file_name.split("_ses-")[1].split("_")[0]


def get_modalities(asset_path):
    """The modalities suffix of a DANDI asset path, empty when the file has none."""
    after_session = asset_path.split("/")[-1].removesuffix(".nwb").split("_ses-")[1]
    return after_session.split("_")[1] if "_" in after_session else ""


def parse_session_id(session_id):
    """The five parts of a session ID."""
    cell_type, state, pharmacology, genotype, date = session_id.split("++")
    return {"cell_type": cell_type, "state": state, "pharmacology": pharmacology, "genotype": genotype, "date": date}


Counter(get_modalities(asset_path) or "(none)" for asset_path in assets)

Counter({'image': 193,

Patch-clamp recordings: one file per mouse and recording day¶

The patch-clamp files hold every cell the lab recorded from one mouse on one day. For each cell they have:

  • One CurrentClampSeries with all its somatic sweeps stored one after another, each at its own start time, and one with its dendritic sweeps when the lab also recorded back-propagating spikes in the dendrites. The stimulus of each sweep is in a matching CurrentClampStimulusSeries.
  • The intracellular recordings table and the tables above it (simultaneous recordings, sequential recordings, repetitions, experimental conditions), which group the sweeps by cell, protocol and condition. Each row of the intracellular recordings table points to its sweep's slice of the series.
  • For dendritic sweeps, two-photon line scans across the dendrite in two dyes: Alexa Fluor 568, which fills the cell and shows its shape, and Fluo-4, which reports calcium.
  • A RecordingsIndexTable in processing/icephys with one row per sweep that gathers the sweep's details, its rows in the tables above and its line-scan slices.

The Sr2+-oEPSC recordings are also patch-clamp files, with voltage-clamp series; they are described in their own section below.

In [4]:
patch_clamp_paths = [asset_path for asset_path in assets if get_modalities(asset_path).startswith("icephys")]
print(f"Patch-clamp files: {len(patch_clamp_paths)}")

cohorts = Counter()
for asset_path in patch_clamp_paths:
    parts = parse_session_id(get_session_id(asset_path))
    cohorts[(parts["cell_type"], parts["state"], parts["pharmacology"], parts["genotype"])] += 1
for (cell_type, state, pharmacology, genotype), count in sorted(cohorts.items()):
    print(f"  {cell_type:5s} {state:18s} {pharmacology:9s} {genotype:10s} {count} files")

The RecordingsIndexTable¶

The quickest way into a file is the RecordingsIndexTable: one row per sweep, with the cell, the condition (named as in the paper's figure legends), the recording site (Soma, or a dendritic site such as Proximal2), the injected current and the sweep's start time.

Reading a sweep¶

Each row of the intracellular recordings table points to its sweep's slice of the cell's series: idx_start and count on the series in the responses column, and the same on the stimulus series in the stimuli column. A stimulus spans its command, so its slice can be shorter or longer than the recording. Here we plot the largest current step of cell 1 in each condition.

In [8]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

recordings_df = nwbfile.intracellular_recordings.to_dataframe()
details = recordings_df["intracellular_recordings"]
somatic_df = recordings_df[(details["cell_id"] == 1) & (details["site"] == "Soma")]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 5), sharex=True, sharey="row", height_ratios=[3, 1])
for column, (condition, condition_df) in enumerate(somatic_df.groupby(("intracellular_recordings", "condition"))):
    row = condition_df.loc[condition_df[("intracellular_recordings", "stimulus_current_pA")].idxmax()]
    response = row[("responses", "response")]
    stimulus = row[("stimuli", "stimulus")]
    time_s = response.timestamps - response.timestamps[0]
    axes[0, column].plot(time_s, response.data * response.timeseries.conversion * 1e3, lw=0.8)
    # The stimulus spans the command, which can end before the recording does
    stimulus_time_s = stimulus.timestamps - response.timestamps[0]
    axes[1, column].plot(stimulus_time_s, stimulus.data * stimulus.timeseries.conversion * 1e12, color="gray")
    axes[0, column].set_title(f"Cell 1, {condition}")
    axes[1, column].set_xlabel("Time from sweep start (s)")
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("Membrane potential (mV)")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Current (pA)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Series: {response.timeseries.name}, {response.timeseries.data.shape[0]} samples for all its sweeps")
print(f"This sweep: samples {response.idx_start} to {response.idx_start + response.count}")

Series: CurrentClampSeriesCell1Somatic, 420000 samples for all its sweeps
This sweep: samples 410000 to 420000

Dendritic excitability: line scans¶

In the dendritic recordings the lab injected brief current pulses at the soma to evoke back-propagating spikes and imaged a line across a dendrite, close to the soma (proximal) or far from it (distal), at high speed. Each dendritic sweep has:

  • Source images in acquisition/ImageLineScanSource: a snapshot of the field of view in each dye at each trial, for example ImageAlexa568Cell1Proximal2Trial1.
  • Line scans in acquisition: the intensity along the line over time, one series per cell, site and dye with the site's trials in recording order, each at its own start time, for example LineScanFluo4Cell1Proximal2. The description gives the line's end points on the source images.
  • ROI responses in processing/ophys/Fluorescence: the mean intensity over the pixels of the line that Prairie View averages into its line profile (the first 17, as a rule), for example RoiResponseSeriesFluo4Cell1Proximal2.
  • Those pixels, the ROI, in processing/ophys/ImageSegmentation: one table per dye with one row per scan line, named in roi_name like the series, for example row Cell1Proximal2 of PlaneSegmentationFluo4.

The line_scan_alexa568, line_scan_fluo4, roi_response_alexa568 and roi_response_fluo4 columns of the RecordingsIndexTable point to each sweep's slices.

In [11]:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
from scipy.signal import butter, filtfilt

cell_id = 1
site = "Proximal2"
trial = 1  # the site's trials are numbered in recording order

site_df = index_df[(index_df["cell_id"] == cell_id) & (index_df["site"] == site)].sort_values("sweep_start_time_s")
trial_row = site_df.iloc[trial - 1]

source_image = nwbfile.acquisition["ImageLineScanSource"].images[f"ImageAlexa568Cell{cell_id}{site}Trial{trial}"]
source_array = np.asarray(source_image.data, dtype=float).T  # NWB images are indexed (x, y)

line_scan = trial_row["line_scan_fluo4"]
line_scan_data = np.asarray(line_scan.data, dtype=float)

roi_response = trial_row["roi_response_fluo4"]
roi_response_data = np.asarray(roi_response.data[:, 0], dtype=float)  # one column, for the one ROI
time_s = roi_response.timestamps - roi_response.timestamps[0]
sampling_rate = 1 / np.mean(np.diff(time_s))

# A first-order Butterworth low-pass at 10 Hz smooths the calcium signal
b, a = butter(1, 10.0 / (0.5 * sampling_rate), btype="low")
roi_response_filtered = filtfilt(b, a, roi_response_data)

# The pixels of the ROI on the source image, indexed (x, y) like the image
roi_x, roi_y = np.nonzero(roi_response.timeseries.rois[0]["image_mask"].iloc[0])

alexa568_cmap = mcolors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("alexa568", ["black", "#FF4500"])
fluo4_cmap = mcolors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("fluo4", ["white", "#32CD32"])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 8))
grid = fig.add_gridspec(nrows=2, ncols=2, hspace=0.3, wspace=0.25)

ax_source = fig.add_subplot(grid[:, 0])
ax_source.imshow(source_array, cmap=alexa568_cmap)
ax_source.plot(roi_x, roi_y, "yellow", linewidth=3, alpha=0.9, label="ROI")
ax_source.set_title(f"Alexa Fluor 568 source image, cell {cell_id} {site} trial {trial}")
ax_source.legend()

ax_line_scan = fig.add_subplot(grid[0, 1])
ax_line_scan.imshow(
    line_scan_data.T,
    cmap=fluo4_cmap,
    aspect="auto",
    origin="lower",
    extent=[0, time_s[-1], 0, line_scan_data.shape[1]],
)
ax_line_scan.set_title("Fluo-4 line scan")
ax_line_scan.set_xlabel("Time from sweep start (s)")
ax_line_scan.set_ylabel("Position along the line (pixels)")

ax_roi = fig.add_subplot(grid[1, 1])
ax_roi.plot(time_s, roi_response_data, color="#A5D6A7", linewidth=0.5, label="Raw")
ax_roi.plot(time_s, roi_response_filtered, color="#1B5E20", linewidth=1.5, label="Low-pass 10 Hz")
ax_roi.set_title("Fluo-4 mean over the ROI")
ax_roi.set_xlabel("Time from sweep start (s)")
ax_roi.set_ylabel("Fluorescence (a.u.)")
ax_roi.legend()
plt.show()

Behaviour: AIM ratings and videos¶

The behaviour files hold one levodopa session of one mouse: the abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) ratings and the videos filmed to count contralateral rotations. Their session ID starts with pan, and their suffix is image when the session has videos.

  • nwbfile.events["aim_scores"] has one row per rated category and observation: the time after the levodopa injection, the category (axial, limb, orolingual, or the lab's total) and the score.
  • processing/behavior/AimEthogram is the catalogue of the rating scheme: what each category and score means.
  • The HED (Hierarchical Event Descriptors) tags of each rating are on aim_scores: the tags of each category in the meanings table of its behavior column, nwbfile.events["aim_scores"].get_meanings_for_column("behavior"), and those of the score on the score column.
  • The videos are ImageSeries in acquisition whose frames stay in the video files next to the NWB file on DANDI.
In [12]:

Sr2+-oEPSC recordings¶

In these experiments the lab expressed channelrhodopsin in motor cortex and recorded SPNs in voltage clamp in a solution where strontium replaces calcium. A blue LED flash on the cortical terminals then evokes asynchronous excitatory postsynaptic currents, whose amplitude measures the strength of single corticostriatal synapses.

The files hold one mouse and recording day each, like the other patch-clamp files:

  • One VoltageClampSeries per cell with its sweeps one after another, each at its own start time, and the intracellular recordings table pointing to each sweep's slice.
  • nwbfile.intervals["optogenetic_pulses_table"]: the time of each LED flash, the cell recorded during it and the LED setting.
  • The light source, the virus and its injection site in nwbfile.lab_meta_data["optogenetic_experiment_metadata"].
In [16]:
oepsc_path = (
    "sub-Subject20230705LIDONtDTomato/"
    "sub-Subject20230705LIDONtDTomato_ses-dSPN++OnState++none++WT++20230705_icephys.nwb"
)
oepsc_nwbfile = open_nwbfile(oepsc_path)
print(list(oepsc_nwbfile.acquisition))
print()
print(oepsc_nwbfile.acquisition["VoltageClampSeriesCell1"].description)

['VoltageClampSeriesCell1', 'VoltageClampSeriesCell2']

Whole-cell voltage-clamp current from cell 1, held at -70 mV (paper Methods). Each 1 s sweep has one blue LED flash at 20 ms (see the optogenetic pulses table) and a -5 mV, 50 ms command step at 920 ms. The paper counted asynchronous events from 40 ms to 400 ms after each flash onset (Methods, Data acquisition and statistical analysis). The 10 sweeps are stored one after another, each at its start time (the sweep_start_time column of the intracellular recordings table), so the pauses between sweeps are kept in the timestamps.

Sweeps with the flash and the analysis window¶

The paper counted the asynchronous events from 40 ms to 400 ms after each flash (Methods). We plot two sweeps of cell 1 with the flash and that window, aligned on the sweep start.

In [18]:
oepsc_recordings_df = oepsc_nwbfile.intracellular_recordings.to_dataframe()
cell_1_df = oepsc_recordings_df[oepsc_recordings_df[("intracellular_recordings", "cell_id")] == 1]
cell_1_pulses = pulses_df[pulses_df["cell_id"] == 1]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, sweep in zip(axes, (0, 6)):
    row = cell_1_df.iloc[sweep]
    response = row[("responses", "response")]
    sweep_start = row[("intracellular_recordings", "sweep_start_time")]
    time_ms = (response.timestamps - response.timestamps[0]) * 1e3
    current_pA = response.data * response.timeseries.conversion * 1e12

    # The flash of this sweep
    flash = cell_1_pulses[(cell_1_pulses["start_time"] >= sweep_start)].iloc[0]
    flash_start_ms = (flash["start_time"] - sweep_start) * 1e3
    flash_stop_ms = (flash["stop_time"] - sweep_start) * 1e3

    ax.plot(time_ms, current_pA, lw=0.6)
    ax.axvspan(flash_start_ms, flash_stop_ms, color="cyan", label="LED flash")
    ax.axvspan(flash_start_ms + 40, flash_start_ms + 400, color="gray", alpha=0.15, label="40 to 400 ms after the flash")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 500)
    ax.set_title(f"Cell 1, sweep {sweep + 1}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Time from sweep start (ms)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Current (pA)")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Event detection¶

As an example of analysis, we detect inward events in the 40 to 400 ms window. A running median over 20 ms follows the slow decay of the synchronous current, and an event is a drop below it of more than five robust standard deviations, estimated with the median absolute deviation (MAD). Crossings within 5 ms are merged into one event. This simple detector is for illustration; the paper's Methods describe the lab's analysis.

In [19]:
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter


def merge_nearby_events(event_times, event_amplitudes, merge_distance_ms):
    """Merge events within merge_distance_ms of each other, keeping the largest amplitude."""
    order = np.argsort(event_times)
    times = np.asarray(event_times)[order]
    amplitudes = np.asarray(event_amplitudes)[order]
    merged_times, merged_amplitudes = [], []
    start = 0
    while start < len(times):
        stop = start + 1
        while stop < len(times) and times[stop] - times[start] <= merge_distance_ms:
            stop += 1
        largest = start + int(np.argmax(amplitudes[start:stop]))
        merged_times.append(times[largest])
        merged_amplitudes.append(amplitudes[largest])
        start = stop
    return np.array(merged_times), np.array(merged_amplitudes)


def detect_inward_events(row, pulses_of_cell, window_ms=(40, 400), threshold_mad=5, merge_distance_ms=5.0):
    """Inward events of one sweep in the window after its flash: times (ms after the flash) and amplitudes (pA)."""
    response = row[("responses", "response")]
    sweep_start = row[("intracellular_recordings", "sweep_start_time")]
    flash = pulses_of_cell[pulses_of_cell["start_time"] >= sweep_start].iloc[0]
    rate = round(1 / (response.timestamps[1] - response.timestamps[0]))
    time_ms = np.arange(response.count) / rate * 1e3 - (flash["start_time"] - sweep_start) * 1e3
    current_pA = response.data * response.timeseries.conversion * 1e12

    # Deviation from a 20 ms running median, which follows the slow decay of the synchronous current
    deviation = current_pA - median_filter(current_pA, size=int(0.02 * rate))
    in_window = (time_ms >= window_ms[0]) & (time_ms <= window_ms[1])
    robust_std = 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(deviation[in_window] - np.median(deviation[in_window])))
    crossings = in_window & (deviation < -threshold_mad * robust_std)
    return merge_nearby_events(time_ms[crossings], -deviation[crossings], merge_distance_ms)


event_times, event_amplitudes = detect_inward_events(cell_1_df.iloc[0], cell_1_pulses)
print(f"Sweep 1 of cell 1: {len(event_times)} events, median amplitude {np.median(event_amplitudes):.1f} pA")

Sweep 1 of cell 1: 4 events, median amplitude 13.7 pA

# Every sweep of cell 1
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(18, 6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
all_amplitudes = []
for ax, (_, row) in zip(axes.ravel(), cell_1_df.iterrows()):
    response = row[("responses", "response")]
    sweep_start = row[("intracellular_recordings", "sweep_start_time")]
    flash = cell_1_pulses[cell_1_pulses["start_time"] >= sweep_start].iloc[0]
    time_ms = (response.timestamps - flash["start_time"]) * 1e3
    event_times, event_amplitudes = detect_inward_events(row, cell_1_pulses)
    all_amplitudes.extend(event_amplitudes)

    current_pA = response.data * response.timeseries.conversion * 1e12
    ax.plot(time_ms, current_pA, lw=0.5)
    ax.plot(event_times, np.interp(event_times, time_ms, current_pA), "r.", markersize=5)
    ax.axvspan(40, 400, color="gray", alpha=0.15)
    ax.set_xlim(-20, 450)
    ax.set_title(f"Sweep at {sweep_start:.0f} s: {len(event_times)} events", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("Time from the flash (ms)")
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("Current (pA)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Cell 1: {len(all_amplitudes)} events, median amplitude {np.median(all_amplitudes):.1f} pA")

Cell 1: 46 events, median amplitude 14.4 pA

Acetylcholine release: GRAB-ACh3.0 imaging¶

The lab imaged the acetylcholine sensor GRAB-ACh3.0 in slices of the dorsolateral striatum while stimulating locally with an electrode, in unlesioned mice, 6-OHDA-lesioned mice and mice in the LID off-state. Each region was filmed in a series of trials while the drug in the bath changed, and was calibrated with acetylcholine (maximum fluorescence) and tetrodotoxin (minimum).

The files hold one mouse and recording day each:

  • One TwoPhotonSeries per region and channel with the region's trials back to back: GRAB-ACh3.0 fluorescence, and the Dodt contrast image of the tissue.
  • One RoiResponseSeries per region and channel in processing/ophys/Fluorescence: the brightness of the whole frame that Prairie View computed during recording.
  • The trials table: one row per trial, with the region, the drug, the stimulation, the stimulus time, and each trial's slices of the series.

Fluorescence of a region's trials¶

Each trial's row points to its slice of the region's fluorescence in the roi_response_grabach3 column. We plot the single-pulse trials of one region in each drug, aligned on the stimulus.

In [24]:
region = trials_df["region"].iloc[0]
single_pulse_df = trials_df[(trials_df["region"] == region) & (trials_df["stimulation"] == "single 1 ms pulse")]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, single_pulse_df["drug"].nunique(), figsize=(15, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, (drug, drug_df) in zip(axes, single_pulse_df.groupby("drug")):
    for _, trial in drug_df.iterrows():
        fluorescence = trial["roi_response_grabach3"]
        ax.plot(fluorescence.timestamps - trial["stimulus_start_time"], fluorescence.data, lw=1)
    ax.axvline(0, color="r", linestyle="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{region}, {drug}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Time from stimulus (s)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("GRAB-ACh3.0 fluorescence (a.u.)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The movie frames of a trial are in its two_photon_grabach3 slice. Here is the mean frame of the first trial.
